title.en: Describe the composition of plant and algal cell walls.

say.en: Put a raisin in water and it swells; put it in strong sugar syrup and it shrinks. Something around every cell decides what goes in and out. In this lesson: Describe the fluid mosaic model.
Distinguish passive and active transport.
Describe the composition of plant and algal cell walls.

body.en: The cell membrane is mainly lipids (chiefly phosphoglycerides) arranged as a bilayer, with polar heads facing out and hydrophobic tails inside, plus proteins and carbohydrates; cholesterol is also present. In the human RBC membrane about 52% is protein and 40% lipid. Proteins are integral (buried in the membrane) or peripheral (on the surface). Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed the *fluid mosaic model*: the quasi-fluid lipid lets proteins move laterally. This fluidity matters for cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

points.en: Passive transport: movement along the concentration gradient by simple diffusion; osmosis is the diffusion of water.
Polar molecules need carrier proteins to cross.
Active transport uses ATP to move against the gradient, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

narration.en: Let us draw the plasma membrane and the ways things cross it.

say.en: The membrane is a lipid bilayer. The polar heads face the water outside and inside; the non-polar tails hide in the middle.
Proteins float in the lipid like tiles in a mosaic. Integral proteins span the membrane; peripheral proteins sit on its surface.
Lipids move sideways, so the membrane is quasi-fluid. That fluidity lets cells grow, divide, secrete and take in material.
Small neutral molecules diffuse down the gradient. Polar molecules need carrier proteins. Active transport moves solutes against the gradient using ATP.
Plant cells also have a wall. Neighbouring cells are glued by the middle lamella of calcium pectate; the secondary wall forms inside the primary wall.
Let us draw the plasma membrane and the ways things cross it.

caption.en: Molecules move down their concentration gradient until both sides are equal (passive transport, no ATP). Small non-polar O2 passes through the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion. Glucose needs a carrier protein and ions need a channel protein (facilitated diffusion).

body.en: Fungi and plants have a rigid non-living *cell wall* outside the plasma membrane. It gives shape, protects from mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and is a barrier to undesirable macromolecules. Algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals like calcium carbonate; plant walls contain cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins. A young cell has a primary wall that can grow; the secondary wall forms on its inner side. The middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, glues neighbouring cells, and plasmodesmata connect their cytoplasm.

points.en: Primary wall: capable of growth, gradually diminishes as the cell matures.

problem.en: The membrane of a human red blood cell contains about 52% protein and 40% lipid. Which component is more abundant, and what model explains how these proteins can move?

steps.en: 52% protein is greater than 40% lipid, so protein is more abundant by weight in the RBC membrane.
The quasi-fluid lipid bilayer allows proteins to move laterally within it.
This is the fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson (1972).
